en: "I alone am the supreme Brahman, the imperishable one known as Vāsudeva"—one who is certain of this is liberated; otherwise, one remains bound. (1)
"O mind, let it be firmly resolved with effort that I alone am the Supreme Brahman, because of my nature as consciousness, my state of non-attachment, and my invincibility. (2)
"I alone am the Supreme Brahman, and I am not separate from Brahman"—
thus should a Brāhmaṇa, established in Brahman, meditate.
Having realized that "I am that Brahman"— the consciousness that is eternally free from all limiting adjuncts— how could one still belong to a caste or stage of life?
"I am Brahman"—he who knows this becomes all this;
the gods are not masters over one's non-existence, for he indeed becomes their very Self. 5.
"He who worships another deity, thinking 'He is one and I am another,' that man does not know Brahman; he is like a beast among the gods. (6)
I am the Self and not another; I am Brahman alone, not subject to sorrow.
I am of the nature of existence, consciousness, and bliss, possessing an eternally liberated essence.
For those who dwell constantly regarding themselves as Brahman,
there is no evil deed whatsoever, nor any calamities arising from evil deeds.
Having constantly realized oneself as Brahman, one should dwell in happiness;
he who performs the contemplation of the Self, thinking "I am Brahman," for even a moment [attains liberation].
It destroys that great sin just as the rising sun dispels darkness;
for through ignorance of Brahman, one perceives the Self, which is like space, as being comparable to a bubble.
From space, wind was produced; from wind, fire; from that, water;
from water, the earth was born; and from that, rice, barley, and so forth.
Earth is in water, water in fire, fire in air, and that air is in space; space is in the unmanifest, and that is in the Pure; I am Hari, the Pure.
I am Viṣṇu, I am Viṣṇu, I am Viṣṇu; I am Hari.
All that consists of the agent, the enjoyer, and so forth, arises solely from ignorance (avidyā).
I am Acyuta, I am Ananta, I am Govinda, I am Hari;
I am Ānanda, I am Aśeṣa, I am the Unborn, and I am the Immortal.
I am eternal, I am free from conceptual construction, I am formless and immutable;
I am of the nature of existence, consciousness, and bliss, and I transcend the five sheaths.
I am the non-doer, the non-enjoyer, the unattached Supreme Lord;
by my constant presence, every sense organ functions.
I am free from beginning, middle, and end; I am never bound.
Pure by nature and stainless, I am that very Self—of this there is no doubt.
One should contemplate: "I am indeed Brahman, not a transmigrating being; I am liberated.
If one is unable to maintain this contemplation, one should constantly repeat this statement.
Through the practice of which that state comes to be, just like the bee-worm;
having abandoned all doubt in this matter, one should practice with firm resolve. (19)
Through the yoga of meditation, one removes the sin of killing a Brahmin within one month;
by constant practice for a year, one shall attain the eight supernatural powers (aṣṭasiddhi).
Through constant practice throughout one's entire life, an ascetic shall become liberated while living:
"I am neither the body, nor the vital breaths, nor likewise the senses. (21)
I am not the mind, nor the intellect, nor indeed the heart, nor the ego;
I am neither earth, nor water, nor fire, nor likewise air.
I am neither space nor sound, nor touch, nor likewise taste;
I am neither smell nor form, nor am I illusion, nor the cycle of worldly existence.
Because I am always of the nature of the witness, I am indeed Śiva alone;
everything has arisen in me alone, and everything is established in me. (24)
Everything merges into me; therefore, I am that non-dual Brahman.
I am omniscient, I am infinite, the Lord of all, and possessed of all powers.
"Ānanda, I am the realization of Truth"—this is the contemplation of Brahman:
"This phenomenal world is indeed false; I am the imperishable, true Brahman. (26)
In this matter, the authority consists of the Vedāntas, the gurus, and likewise personal experience:
"I am Brahman alone, not a transmigrating being; nor am I separate from Brahman. (27)
I am not the body, nor is the body mine; I am the absolute, eternal one.
Indeed, there is only the one, the beginningless and non-dual Brahman; here there is nothing else whatsoever.
In the center of the lotus of the heart, like a lamp, is the essence of the Vedas, consisting of the syllable Om, inconceivable and accessible through meditation by yogis;
it is the union of Hari, Guru, and Śiva, the one who dwells within all beings.
He who contemplates this even once with his mind is indeed liberated. || 29 ||
Thus ends "The Contemplation on Brahman" composed by the venerable Śaṅkarācārya.
